# Why is my backtest lying?

*You'll need passive orders and fills (chapter 2), why making earns (chapter 4) and adverse selection (chapter 5).*

## The story

In Prosperity 4 a team that calls itself Kayzerjali tuned one product, Pepper Root, in the competition's open
backtester. Over one window of 100,000 timestamps it made +2,415. The same code, on the same window, on the live
platform, made +436 (*their claim*). They didn't conclude that the strategy was bad. They concluded that the backtester's
fill model "diverges severely from the live platform", and rebuilt their loop around it: the live result became the
only thing they optimised, and the backtester became a check for bugs before an upload
[(`references/online-snapshots/Kayzerjali_Prosperity2026/run_cycle.md:3-7`)]{.src}.

A Prosperity 3 team, Frankfurt Hedgehogs, said the same thing more politely. Their backtester was "very accurate and
highly flexible", but it "could not … accurately model potential fill probabilities after inserting liquidity for
assets like Rainforest Resin and Kelp" [(`references/prosperity3-frankfurt-hedgehogs/README.md:898-900`)]{.src}.

Both teams hit the same wall, and it is not a bug in anyone's code. It is a question that recorded data cannot answer.

## The idea

A backtest replays a recorded day: every tick's order book and every trade that printed. Our bot reads each tick and
sends orders, and the engine decides what would have happened to them. Some of that is easy. An order that crosses the
book, buying at or above the best ask, trades with orders that were really there, at their prices: that is a *take*,
and the replay knows the answer. The hard part is everything else.

A market maker's income comes mostly from orders that *don't* cross: a bid below the best ask and an ask above the best
bid, waiting for someone to trade with them. These are *passive* orders. When the recording shows a trade at our bid's
price, would it have traded with us? The recording can't say, because we weren't there. That trade happened between two
other bots. If we had been there, the seller might have hit us instead, or might have hit the other bot first, or might
not have traded at all because our order changed the book it saw.

So every backtest engine answers the question by assumption, and the assumption is a setting. Ours has four main ones,
and @fig-fill-modes shows what they do to one bot on the same three days.

- **`all`** (the default, which matches the open-source Prosperity backtester): a recorded trade at our price, or
  through it, fills us.
- **`worse`**: only a trade strictly through our price fills us. If someone sold below our bid, they would surely have
  sold to us first.
- **`none`**: no recorded trades at all; only orders in the visible book fill us.
- **`resting`**: orders stay in the book between ticks and wait in a queue behind the orders that were already at
  their price, so a trade at our price fills whoever was there first.

![The template on Prosperity 3's round 1, all three days, under each fill model. Resting uses the default queue
[(`back`, behind everyone already there)]{.src}. Data: `data/fill_modes.csv`, from
`arena.backtest python/bots/template.py 1 --data p3` in each mode.](figures/f09_fill_modes.png){#fig-fill-modes
fig-alt="Bar chart of profit over three days under four fill models: all 72,674, worse 63,302, none 28,217, resting 66,558."}

The bot is the same, and so are the days. The answer goes from 28,217 to 72,674. More than half of the default number
comes from fills that only exist if you believe that bots which traded with each other would have traded with us
instead [(`README.md`, "Fill assumptions matter")]{.src}.

### Why the error isn't noise

If the fill model were only imprecise, it would cost some accuracy and nothing else. It is worse than that: it is
biased, and the bias depends on the very parameters you tune.

Take Kelp's `make_edge`, how far from our fair value the bot quotes. On Prosperity 3's round 1, the template made, in
thousands:

| `make_edge` | 0.5 | 1 | 1.5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| under `all` | 72.7 | 81.3 | 84.5 |
| under `worse` | 63.3 | 57.8 | 52.3 |
| out of sample (round 5), `all` | 53.9 | 61.2 | 64.6 |
| out of sample (round 5), `worse` | 48.8 | 44.2 | 38.8 |

::: {.content-visible when-format="audio"}
On round 1, a wider quote makes more under the optimistic rule, 72.7 thousand at half a tick up to 84.5 thousand at one
and a half, and less under the strict rule, 63.3 down to 52.3. On three days of round 5 that the choice never saw, the
same happens: 53.9 up to 64.6 under the optimistic rule, 48.8 down to 38.8 under the strict one.
:::

Under `all`, the wider quote wins; under `worse`, it loses. And it isn't overfitting to three days: on round 5, which
the choice never saw, each fill model ranks the edges the same way it did in sample [(`IDEAS.md`, "Why the zoo beat the
template head to head")]{.src}. Held-out data can't settle it, because the held-out days are replayed under the same
assumption. **The fill model decides the edge.** A permutation test agrees: shuffling the order of Kelp's ticks finds
the same best edge and the same lift over the median setting (p 0.55), so the choice comes from each tick's book and
the fill rule, not from anything the price does over time [(`IDEAS.md`, "A permutation test of the whole search")]{.src}.

The reason is mechanical. A quote further from the fair sits where fewer traders reach, so a larger share of its fills
are the doubtful kind, trades printed at its price between other bots. The rule that counts those as ours rewards
moving out; the rule that doesn't punishes it.

### The other things a replay assumes

The fill rule is the largest assumption, not the only one. Each of these is a setting in our engine, each was measured
on Prosperity data, and none can be read from the data itself:

- **When an order arrives.** The replay matches an order against the book the bot saw. If the exchange applies it a
  tick later, the price has moved. The template on round 1 falls from 72,674 to 40,472 one tick late: Resin's takes
  against its fixed fair arrive after the price has already come back [(`IDEAS.md`, "Orders that arrive a tick late";
  `--delay`)]{.src}.
- **Whether what we take stays gone.** A replay usually restores the recorded book every tick, so the volume we bought
  is back for sale a tick later. In our first rehearsal the bot made 42,446 on the hidden days with the book restored,
  and 31,172 when what it took stayed gone: a quarter of the score from one assumption [(`IDEAS.md`, "The kickoff
  prompts on a disguised round"; `--deplete`)]{.src}.
- **Whether orders rest.** With orders that live one tick, plain market making on Prosperity 3's jumpy basket legs
  earned a few thousand each. Let the same quotes rest, and the next snapshot jumps straight through them, filling them
  at their own stale price: Roses lost 1,477k [(`IDEAS.md`, "Market making on products that jump, with resting
  orders")]{.src}.
- **What the position is worth at the end.** A bot that ends the day holding something is scored on cash plus that
  position at some price, and the engine chooses which:

  [$\text{PnL} = \text{cash} + \text{position} \times \text{mark}$]{speak="profit is the cash, plus the position valued at the mark"}

  The mark can be the mid, the last trade or a portal's own average (the Varde rehearsal used the average of the last
  100 trades, and didn't say so). The `--mark` option picks one.

### What to do about it

Three habits follow, and the repo is built around them.

1. **Never trust one fill model.** Run every comparison under at least two, `all` and `worse`, and believe only what
   wins under both [(`README.md`, "Fill assumptions matter")]{.src}. If the ranking flips, the gain is a property of the
   assumption.
2. **Measure the real exchange early.** One upload of a plain bot tells you how far the portal is from each of your
   settings. That is chapter 8's tool, calibrate, and the playground before round 1 is the cheapest place to use it.
3. **Prefer the edges a replay can see.** A take against the visible book is filled the same way under every rule;
   income from passive fills is the part to doubt.

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
A backtest is a simulator, and the fill model is its sim-to-real gap. Two things make it worse than the usual gap.
It is *one-sided*: optimistic fills always look better, so a search drifts toward whatever the simulator flatters. And
it is *correlated with the parameters*: `make_edge` decides how many of your fills are the doubtful kind, so tuning
it is tuning to the gap. Held-out days don't help, as they would against overfitting, because they share the
simulator. The fix is the one for any simulator: measure it against the real system and treat the remaining
uncertainty as a range, here the span between `all` and `worse`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="In the repo"}
- The fill rules: `uv run python -m arena.backtest BOT DAYS --match-trades all|worse|none`, `--resting` with
  `--queue back|prob|front`, `--fill-ratio`, `--delay`, `--deplete`, `--mark mid|touch|last`
  (`python/arena/engine.py`; `ARCHITECTURE.md`, "Matching rules (Prosperity semantics)").
- Two models at once in a grid: `arena.grid ... --modes all,worse`; named bundles with `--scenario`.
- The rows: `IDEAS.md`'s "The template's market maker" (every fill mode), "Why the zoo beat the template head to
  head", "Orders that arrive a tick late".
:::

::: {.callout-important title="On the day"}
`RUNBOOK.md`, "Each round", T+1:00: the grid runs under the mode closest to the rules *and* `worse`, until the rules or
the playground's fills pin the mode down. `ON_THE_DAY.md`, "Which backtest settings match the playground?", says how
to read the first upload against our settings.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper" appearance="simple"}
- Bouchaud et al., *Trades, Quotes and Prices*, ch. 21 §21.3–21.4 (PDF pp. 413–421): limit against market orders, the
  value of a place in the queue, and why backtests with phantom orders are biased.
- DeLise, *The negative drift of a limit order fill* (28 pp.): why the fills you get are, on average, the ones you
  wouldn't have wanted. That is chapter 5's subject, and the reason `worse` is closer to the truth than it looks.
:::
